errors.english: the Tathagata [note: The Buddha] caused his body to be illuminated with supreme clarity. Out of devotion, he performed the funeral rites
errors.why: 'Supremely illuminating' is an epithet of the Tathāgata, and 'to his body' is the object of the devoted worship (gus pas mchod mdzad); the Buddha did not make the body shine.

fix.find: caused his body to be illuminated with supreme clarity. Out of devotion, he performed the funeral rites
fix.replace: who supremely illuminates, out of devotion performed worship to his body

errors.english: even by the Teachers of the world
errors.why: The Tibetan says parents are worthy of honour even by the teacher (guru) of the wise, i.e. the Buddha himself, not 'Teachers of the world'.

note: Gist is right, but the Tathāgata's epithet is turned into an action on the corpse and the closing line is blurred.

errors.english: what transgression would there be? It is stated that otherwise the fault is a grave offense.
errors.why: The canonical question-and-answer is 'if he ... withdraws, what offense is it? A sthūlātyaya'; the English turns the question into a rhetorical 'no offense' and invents 'otherwise'.

fix.find: what transgression would there be? It is stated that otherwise the fault is a grave offense.
fix.replace: what offense does he incur? It is stated: a grave offense.

note: A careful technical Vinaya rendering, but one key ruling is reversed.

errors.english: is capable of being established without depending on other things—these being the two aspects of the object and the object in relation to cognition
errors.why: The substance is what can accomplish, independently, the two kinds of purpose (the object's own and that connected with cognition); the English misreads it as the substance being 'established'.

errors.english: Qualities are those conditioned things whose characteristics, such as impermanence, are distinguished
errors.why: Qualities are the distinguishing features (impermanence etc.) attached to those conditioned things, not the conditioned things themselves.

note: Generally sound, with two clauses on substance and quality misparsed.

errors.english: one should be willing to give up their body for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
errors.why: The a fortiori clause 'how much more so a single [body/life]' is dropped.

note: A faithful rendering of the Sadāprarudita excerpt as cited in the commentary.

errors.english: [note: The Conqueror, the Blessed One, spoke those words in order to instruct the monks: "This is the second leaf, the Legend of Shrisena, from the *Vine of the Bodhisattva's Legends* composed by Kshemendra."]
errors.why: The Sanskrit is the verse's last line plus Kṣemendra's colophon; the note puts the colophon in the Buddha's mouth.

fix.find: [note: The Conqueror, the Blessed One, spoke those words in order to instruct the monks: "This is the second leaf, the Legend of Shrisena, from the *Vine of the Bodhisattva's Legends* composed by Kshemendra."]
fix.replace: [note: the Sanskrit gives the last line of the verse and the colophon: the second leaf, the Legend of Śrīsena, in Kṣemendra's Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā.]

errors.english: The Gem of a Man was born into this world of Bliss-Goers [note: the realm of the Buddhas].
errors.why: Some jewel of a man who makes manifest the Sugata (prakaṭitasugatiḥ) is born in the world (jagati); there is no 'world of Bliss-Goers'.

errors.english:
Which possesses the pure radiance of those who perform merit,
Whose nature is like the Ganges in its strength of heart,
It remains within a stainless mind.
errors.why: The verse says the city was inhabited, as if by sacred fords, by pure merit-makers full of radiance and goodness, with minds stainless as the Ganges; the English makes the city the subject and loses the inhabitants.

note: The colophon is garbled into a note and the opening kāvya verses are only loosely construed.
A faithful rendering of the Mahāyāna-authenticity argument and the transmission list.

errors.english: Because it is not connected to many, it would become many; otherwise, it could not be one.
errors.why: The point is that, being connected with many, the whole would be many, so it cannot be one; the English adds a negation and inverts the argument.

fix.find: Because it is not connected to many, it would become many; otherwise, it could not be one.
fix.replace: Because it is connected with many, it would be many; so it could not be one.

errors.english: the logical absurdity that it would reside within itself would follow without hindrance
errors.why: The consequence is the question 'where then does it itself reside?', not that it resides within itself.

note: Follows the anti-avayavin argument well except for one inverted conclusion.

errors.english: The quality of possession, being an attribute itself,
errors.why: ldan pa here is Vaiśeṣika saṃyoga, 'conjunction' (a guṇa), rendered throughout as 'possession', which obscures the whole argument about variegated conjunction.

fix.find: The quality of possession, being an attribute itself,

errors.english: the object of sound is not diverse in nature
errors.why: sgra'i yul is the referent of the word ['variegated'], namely conjunction, which is not itself of variegated nature; it has nothing to do with sound.
The reason is 'because each would be variegated', a consequence against the opponent, not a statement that the parts are distinct.

note: The key Vaiśeṣika term saṃyoga is consistently mistranslated, so the argument structure is hard to follow.

errors.english: how is it possible to avoid this very fault?
errors.why: The Tibetan instructs that the same fault applies to simultaneous or later arising and is to be refuted as appropriate; it is not a rhetorical question.

note: A faithful rendering including the Akṣayamati quotation.

errors.english: When the mind engages with an entity [note: original: "vastu"], it produces an incompatible cause in the nature of habitual tendencies
errors.why: It is the cognition of non-entity which, by producing an incompatible cause in the form of a latency, cuts off the continued occurrence of the cognition of entity; the English makes the entity-cognition produce the incompatible cause.

errors.english: just as heat is distinct from cold
errors.why: The analogy is 'like cold from fire', i.e. no latency distinct from the manifest concept remains, as no cold remains in the presence of fire; 'heat is distinct from cold' inverts the analogy's point.

note: Usable for this dense Pramāṇavārttika commentary, but the key causal claim about the latency is misassigned.
